To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the three paths for learning analytics implementations are: 1. the path of the “magic bullet” that is unlikely to have a meaningful and sustained impact on learning and learning; 2. the path of “business as usual” that is unlikely, but not impossible, to have a meaningful impact on learning; 3. the path of a “new way of thinking” that can have a meaningful and sustainable impact on learning.
learning analytics is not a panacea, but it can be a useful tool for supporting teaching staff to make better-informed decisions about their students.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: How can learning analytics implementations move beyond rhetoric to provide meaningful and sustained support to learning and teaching in higher education?
how learning analytics can be used to improve learning and teaching in higher education, and how this might be achieved.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
learning analytics is not yet a reality.
the jury is still out, but the signs are promising.
there is no definitive path to learning analytics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are on a path of learning analytics as a tool for learning and teaching.
the project has moved beyond rhetoric and is now in reality.
the learning analytics implementation is moving from the first path to the third path.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the learning analytics path we are on is one that focuses on learning and teaching and the student experience.
learning analytics is a powerful tool for teaching and learning when used as part of a holistic approach to student support, rather than as a standalone technology.
learning analytics can be a powerful tool for enhancing learning and teaching, but it requires significant investment and a long-term commitment from the organisation to realise its potential.
